en: The PAGASA track forecast on its site is support because it tells communities which provinces should prepare first as the cyclone moves.
The Mines and Geosciences Bureau, under DENR, posts landslide-prone maps that authorities use to tell hillside communities when to leave in heavy typhoon rain.
PAGASA storm-surge maps on its site support coastal barangays by showing who should move to higher ground before the cyclone arrives.
PAGASA radar images on the official site help authorities time last-minute warnings, a monitoring support communities depend on during the cyclone.
Wave energy rides wind-driven bumps on the surface; tidal difference is the slower rise and fall from the Moon and Sun, a distinction sources insist on.
Meteor showers return on nearly the same calendar dates each year because Earth crosses the same dusty orbit at the same point in its year.
Inserting or deleting a letter so the reading frame slips is often harmful because many amino acids downstream go wrong.
A Lewis symbol for oxygen shows the letter O with six dots around it, one for each valence electron from group 16.
InSAR uses repeated radar satellite images to map how the ground has displaced between two passes, a process for measuring plate and quake motion.
The Sun gives energy to plants, which make their own food, so every food chain on Earth begins with sunlight.
A herbivore is an animal that eats only plants, like a grasshopper chewing on rice leaves in a field.
An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and animals, like a wild boar digging for roots and small insects.
In a food chain, arrows point from the food to the eater, showing the direction that energy moves.
The second animal in a food chain is called a secondary consumer, and it eats the herbivore, so it is usually a carnivore.
In a rice field, a grasshopper eats the rice leaves, and a spider eats the grasshopper.
In a freshwater pond, tiny algae are eaten by bangus fry, and larger fish eat the bangus fry.
Herbivores have flat teeth for grinding plants, while carnivores have sharp teeth for tearing meat.
A food web is a group of connected food chains, because most animals eat more than one kind of food.
A Philippine long-tailed macaque is an omnivore because it eats fruits, leaves, and also insects and small birds.
If one animal in a food chain disappears, the animals that eat it and the animals it eats are both affected.
The Philippine eagle is a carnivore that hunts monkeys, snakes, and birds, making it a top predator in the forest.
The carabao, or water buffalo, is a large herbivore that eats grasses and leaves, and it is a common sight in Philippine farms.
Weighing a clay ball before and after reshaping shows that changing its shape does not change its mass.
The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, is the invisible boundary where the crust ends and the denser mantle rock begins beneath it.
The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell made of the crust and the stiff top part of the upper mantle.
The asthenosphere is the hot, soft layer below the lithosphere where rock can slowly flow like very thick syrup.
Earth's tectonic plates are pieces of lithosphere that slowly slide over the flowing asthenosphere underneath them.
Oceanic crust is made mostly of basalt, a dark, dense volcanic rock that forms from cooling lava on the seafloor.
Heat from deep inside Earth makes the asthenosphere flow in slow circular currents that help drag the plates above.
Oceanic crust is constantly created at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed at subduction zones, so it is much younger than continental crust.
PHIVOLCS monitors earthquakes and volcanic eruptions in the Philippines, which happen where the lithosphere's plates push against each other.
Carrying capacity is the largest number of living things an area can support with its food, water, and space.
If a population accidentally grows past its carrying capacity, it can crash because the food runs out too quickly.
When prey animals become plentiful, predators increase and eat more of them, which then slows the prey population's growth.
Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees from straight up, and this tilt is what makes sunlight hit different places at different angles.
The equator receives fairly steady sunlight all year because the Sun's direct rays stay near it, so its temperature changes little.
The Tropic of Capricorn is the southernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead, which happens around the December solstice.
During the equinoxes in March and September, the Sun is directly above the equator, and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
In a motor, electricity flowing through a coil inside a magnet gives the coil a push, so it turns.
In a generator, turning a coil inside a magnet pushes electrons along the wire, creating an electric current.
In a hydroelectric plant, falling water spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator to make electricity.
Wind turbines are big generators: wind spins the blades, which spin a coil inside a magnet to produce electricity.
A hand-crank flashlight has a tiny generator that makes electricity when you turn the crank, so no battery is needed.
A bicycle dynamo is a small generator that rubs against the tire to power the headlight while you ride.
Geothermal power plants in Leyte use steam from underground to spin generators and make electricity for many homes.
In a generator, spinning the coil changes the magnetic field around it, which pushes electrons along the wire to make current.
Magnitude is one number that tells how much energy an earthquake releases at its focus, and it stays the same no matter where you feel it.
Each whole number up the magnitude scale means the earthquake releases about 32 times more energy, so a 7 is far stronger than a 6.
A seismograph is an instrument with a weight and a drum that draws wiggly lines to record how the ground moves during an earthquake.
Earthquake waves travel in two main kinds: P-waves arrive first with a push-pull motion, and S-waves arrive later with a side-to-side shake.
In a strike-slip fault, rocks slide past each other sideways along a nearly vertical crack, like two hands rubbing against each other.
A tsunami can travel across deep ocean as fast as a jet plane, about 800 kilometers per hour, but its wave is small and low there.
When a tsunami reaches shallow water near shore, it slows down and piles up into a tall wall of water that can flood the land.
PHIVOLCS uses its own intensity scale from I to X to rate how strongly people in the Philippines feel an earthquake's shaking.
Scientists today mostly use the moment magnitude scale, which works better than the old Richter scale for very large earthquakes.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a belt of active faults and volcanoes where many earthquakes happen every year.
When a big underwater quake shifts the seafloor, the whole column of water above it moves at once, and that push creates a tsunami wave.
A strong earthquake has a high magnitude everywhere, but its intensity can be high near the epicenter and low far away from it.
Shallow-focus earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep-focus ones because their energy has less rock to travel through before reaching the surface.
PHIVOLCS watches earthquakes and sea levels around the Philippines and sends tsunami warnings to coastal communities when a big quake hits the ocean floor.
Taping a small marker on one coil of a slinky shows that the spring itself does not travel; the marker swings in place as the wave passes.
For a longitudinal wave, the wavelength is the distance between two neighboring compressions, measured with a ruler on the stretched spring.
The amplitude of a transverse wave is measured with a ruler as the height from the rest position up to a crest.
A tertiary consumer is a carnivore that eats other carnivores, like a snake that eats a bird which ate a caterpillar.
In a coconut grove, a coconut beetle eats palm leaves, and a monitor lizard eats the beetle, making a three-link food chain.
A fruit bat eats fruits and is a herbivore, while a python that eats the bat is a carnivore, showing a forest food chain.
When energy moves from one step of a food chain to the next, some is lost as heat, so each step has less energy.
A food chain shows the order of eating, but it does not show how much food each animal eats.
The Philippine Trench is a deep underwater canyon where the Philippine Sea Plate dives beneath the archipelago, marking the boundary that shapes the islands' future path.
The Philippines is an island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands built where one plate dives under another.
To compare soft and rigid objects, a class gives each one the same gentle push and watches which one moves or changes shape more.
The crust is the only layer of Earth that humans have directly drilled into, with the deepest hole reaching about 12 kilometers.
The crust is made of three rock families: igneous from cooled magma, sedimentary from pressed layers, and metamorphic from heat and pressure.
Scientists map the crust's hidden layers by measuring how seismic waves from earthquakes travel through it.
A place receives the most intense sunlight when the Sun is directly overhead at noon, because the rays hit the ground at 90 degrees and do not spread out.
The Antarctic Circle is the southern counterpart of the Arctic Circle, where the Sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full day at the solstices.
In the Philippines, the noontime shadow points south when the Sun is north of the zenith, and north when the Sun is south of the zenith.
The plates glide on a softer, partly melted layer called the asthenosphere, which lets them shift slowly over millions of years.
Deep ocean trenches, such as the Philippine Trench, form at the line where a heavy oceanic plate bends and dives downward.
Melting above a sinking oceanic plate feeds arcs of volcanoes, like Mayon in the Philippines, which grow along the plate edge.
At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other, like along the Philippine Fault, grinding without making or destroying crust.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is a giant loop of subduction zones where oceanic plates sink, creating many of Earth's volcanoes and quakes.
PHIVOLCS tracks the movement of plates around the Philippines to warn communities about earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
The Philippines sits in a mobile belt squeezed between two large plates, which is why it has many faults, trenches, and volcanoes.
Slow convection currents in Earth's hot mantle, caused by heat rising and cooling rock sinking, help drag the plates along.
When two continental plates collide, neither is dense enough to sink, so the crust crumples upward into high mountains like the Himalayas.
Scientists calculate an earthquake's magnitude from the size of the wiggles on a seismogram, not from the damage it causes.
A tsunami is a series of waves that can last for hours, and the first wave is often not the biggest one.
Not all tsunamis come from earthquakes; underwater landslides and volcanic eruptions can also push water and create tsunami waves.
Wind makes ordinary ocean waves that only move the surface, but a tsunami moves the whole water column from the seafloor up.
The Philippine Fault is a long crack that runs through the islands, and it can produce strong earthquakes when its blocks slip.
The Marikina Valley Fault runs near Metro Manila, and scientists monitor it because it could move and cause strong shaking.
The focus of an earthquake is also called the hypocenter, the exact underground spot where the rock first breaks.
When a tsunami reaches land, the height of the water on the shore is called run-up, and it can be much taller than the wave in the open ocean.
A fault is a crack in the earth's crust where two blocks of rock can move past each other, and earthquakes happen when they suddenly slip.
The largest earthquakes ever recorded are about magnitude 9, and the magnitude scale has no fixed upper limit.
A tsunami can cross an entire ocean and still have enough energy to flood a coast far from the earthquake that made it.
A generator cannot make electricity by itself; it needs an outside force like falling water, wind, or steam to keep its coil spinning.
The upper continental crust is made of lighter rocks like granite and gneiss, while the lower crust is denser and more like basalt.
When tectonic plates collide, the upper crust is squeezed and lifted to build mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
Sound travels through air as a longitudinal wave, with air molecules bunching together and spreading apart along the direction of travel.
Light is a transverse wave, so it can travel through empty space without needing air or any material to carry it.
To distinguish earthquake waves, read the seismograph: the first arrival is the longitudinal P-wave, and the later one is the transverse S-wave.
Frequency is the number of complete waves that pass a point in one second, and it is measured in units called hertz.
Sound waves need a medium such as air, water, or solid material to travel, so there is no sound in empty space.
A precipitate is a solid that forms when two clear liquids are mixed and react to make a new substance.
A new substance forms because the change is chemical, so the original materials cannot be easily separated back.
In a series circuit, add the voltmeter readings across each load, and the total equals the battery's voltage.
Electricians wire household outlets in parallel so each appliance gets the full voltage and turning off one switch does not shut off the others.
Genotype is the pair of alleles a person carries, while phenotype is the visible result, like having free earlobes or attached earlobes.
A Punnett square is a simple grid that shows all the possible allele combinations a child could inherit from two parents.
A GPS receiver measures the travel time of radio signals from at least four satellites to compute its exact position on Earth.
As a population grows, its waste can make the water or soil more acidic, which harms the organisms and slows their growth.
When two oceanic plates collide, the older and colder plate is denser, so it sinks beneath the younger, warmer plate.
The ocean floor has stripes of normal and reversed magnetism that spread out evenly from mid-ocean ridges, recording seafloor spreading.
The Manila Trench west of Luzon is a subduction zone where the South China Sea floor sinks beneath the Philippine plate.
Large earthquakes happen where oceanic plates sink, because the sinking plate sticks to the plate above it and then suddenly slips.
The islands of the Philippines are pieces of oceanic and continental crust that were welded together by plate collisions over millions of years.
To measure the current in one branch of a parallel circuit, open that branch and insert the ammeter in series with that branch only.
If one parent has two dominant alleles and the other has two recessive alleles, all their children will be carriers.
If one parent has two recessive alleles and the other is a carrier, about half of their children will show the recessive trait and half will be carriers.
A line of people passing a gentle shove from one to the next models a longitudinal wave, because each person leans forward and back while the shove travels along the line.
Melting ice is a physical change because the water can freeze again, but turning limewater cloudy is chemical because the white solid is a new substance.
Coral reefs and seashells are made of calcium carbonate, the same substance that forms when carbon dioxide meets limewater.
A ticker tape timer makes dots on a paper tape as the cart moves, and the spacing of dots shows how speed changes during stopping.
The law of conservation of mass says the total mass of substances before a reaction equals the total mass after, so nothing is lost or gained.
When iron rusts, it gains mass because it combines with oxygen from the air, but the total mass of iron plus oxygen equals the rust.
The arrow in a chemical equation means 'produces' or 'yields', separating the starting reactants on the left from the products on the right.
Scientists use a capital letter for a dominant allele and a lowercase letter for a recessive allele, like D and d.
A Punnett square shows the possible chances for one set of parents, while a pedigree chart shows the actual traits that appeared across many generations.
The carabao, or kalabaw, is a Philippine animal that lives on land, so it is called a terrestrial animal.
The Philippine eagle flies high in the sky and nests on tall trees, so it is an aerial animal.
Rice plants, called palay, grow on land in fields and paddies, so they are terrestrial plants.
Bakawan, or mangroves, grow in salty water along the coast, so they are aquatic plants.
Frogs can live on land and in water, so they are not purely terrestrial or aquatic but amphibious.
A desert is a dry terrestrial habitat where only some plants and animals can survive without much water.
A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, and it provides food, water, and shelter.
A subduction zone is where one tectonic plate dives beneath another, and the big quakes there can push the seafloor and create tsunamis.
After a big offshore earthquake, a tsunami can reach the nearest coast within minutes, so coastal people have very little time to move to higher ground.
The Philippine Trench is a deep underwater crack east of the country where one plate dives under another, and it can cause very large earthquakes.
Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow the main quake, and they happen because the rocks around the fault are still adjusting.
Scientists use pressure sensors on the ocean floor to detect a tsunami passing overhead before it reaches the shore.
A life cycle is the order of stages an animal passes through from its birth until it can produce young of its own.
A butterfly's life cycle has four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and adult butterfly, each looking completely different from the last.
A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, and it supplies everything the living thing needs like food, water, and shelter.
The rice field is a wet habitat where palay, or rice plants, grow in standing water during the planting season.
On the seashore, hermit crabs and sand crabs dig into the wet sand to hide from the sun and from birds.
Mudskippers are fish that can walk and jump on mud, and they are often seen in the roots of mangrove swamps.
In Philippine coastal towns, the seashore habitat provides food and work for people who catch fish and gather shells.
A fair test changes only one thing at a time, while all other conditions stay the same, so the result shows what caused the change.
Taking the same measurement three times and averaging the readings makes the result more trustworthy.
When the tide goes out, water stays in hollows of rocks, and these tide pools shelter small crabs, snails, and tiny fish.
Mangrove swamps act as nurseries for young fish and shrimp, giving them hiding places among the roots until they grow bigger.
Earthworms in a garden eat dead leaves and make tunnels in the soil, which helps air and water reach plant roots.
Sandpipers are shorebirds that run along the beach and poke their beaks into the sand to find worms and small crabs.
The tangled roots of mangrove trees make a maze where small fish can escape from bigger fish that hunt in open water.
Herons and kingfishers build their nests in mangrove trees, where the branches over the water keep their eggs safe from land predators.
The plus sign in an equation means 'and' for listing multiple reactants or products, not a math addition sign.
To describe rusting, scientists write iron plus oxygen yields iron oxide, and they can show the same reaction using chemical formulas.
For photosynthesis, scientists write carbon dioxide and water plus sunlight yield glucose and oxygen, then translate each name into its formula.
The balanced equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, showing 6 carbon atoms on each side.
The tamaraw, a wild buffalo, lives only on Mindoro's grasslands, so it is a terrestrial animal.
The dugong, a sea cow, grazes on seagrass in shallow coastal waters, so it is an aquatic animal.
The Philippine crocodile lives in freshwater rivers and lakes, so it is an aquatic animal.
The Philippine flying lemur glides from tree to tree but does not flap wings, so it is not an aerial animal.
The nipa palm grows in swampy water along coasts, so it is an aquatic plant.
The water hyacinth floats on rivers and ponds, so it is an aquatic plant that drifts with the current.
The Philippine mouse-deer, or pilandok, lives on the forest floor, so it is a terrestrial animal.
The Philippine duck lives near lakes and feeds in water, so it is an aquatic bird.
The Philippine hornbill, or kalaw, is a bird that flies through the forest canopy, so it is an aerial animal.
PHIVOLCS uses seismographs, gas sensors, and satellite images to watch volcanoes and warn communities before an eruption.
Lahar is a fast-moving mudflow of volcanic ash, rock, and water that can rush down river valleys long after an eruption ends.
A pyroclastic flow is a cloud of hot gas, ash, and rock that races down a volcano's slope faster than a car can drive.
The Philippines uses alert levels from 0 to 5 to show how dangerous a volcano is, with 5 meaning a major eruption is happening.
Mayon in Albay is the most active volcano in the Philippines, having erupted more than 50 times in the past 400 years.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone where many of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes happen.
Areas close to a volcano's crater are often permanent danger zones where building homes is not allowed.
Nipa palms grow in the brackish water of Philippine mangrove swamps, and their leaves are used by people to make roofs.
The maya, or rice bird, is a common visitor to Philippine rice fields, where it eats grains of palay as they ripen.
Fiddler crabs live on the mud of mangrove swamps, and the males wave one large claw to attract females.
Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds into a butterfly with wings.
The butterfly's caterpillar sheds its skin several times as it grows bigger before forming a chrysalis.
The Philippine brown deer, or usa, lives in forests on land, so it is a terrestrial animal.
Kangkong, also called water spinach, grows in wet fields and ditches, so it is an aquatic plant.
The Philippine flying fox, a large bat, flies at night to find fruit, so it is an aerial animal.
The narra tree, the national tree of the Philippines, grows on land, so it is a terrestrial plant.
The sampaguita flower, the national flower, grows on a vine on land, so it is a terrestrial plant.
A graduated cylinder measures liquid volume in milliliters, so you know exactly how much liquid to weigh.
Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, giving digestive juices more surface to attack, so digestion works faster.
Salivary glands in the mouth release saliva, which moistens food and begins breaking down starch into sugar.
Waves of muscle called peristalsis squeeze food down the esophagus and through the whole digestive tract, even if you are upside down.
The stomach churns food into a soft liquid called chyme, mixing it with gastric juice to start digesting proteins.
Tiny finger-like villi line the inside of the small intestine and absorb digested nutrients into the blood.
Bile from the liver breaks big fat globules into tiny droplets so fat-digesting enzymes can work on them.
The pancreas releases enzymes into the small intestine that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats from your meal.
The large intestine absorbs water and salts from the leftover food, making the waste more solid before it leaves.
Elimination is the last step, when the rectum and anus push the leftover waste out of the body as feces.
Fiber in vegetables and fruits is not digested, but it helps push food along the intestines and makes waste easier to pass.
A flap called the epiglottis closes over the windpipe when you swallow, so food goes down the esophagus, not the lungs.
A forecaster also marks the point where the typhoon's track leaves the PAR boundary to record the exit time.
The liver and pancreas are accessory organs that send digestive juices into the small intestine, even though food never passes through them.
The gallbladder stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the small intestine when you eat fatty food.
Helpful bacteria in the large intestine make some vitamins, like vitamin K, which the body then absorbs from the waste.
Metamorphosis lets young and adult animals eat different foods, so they do not compete for the same food in the same place.
A butterfly's metamorphosis is complete because its caterpillar looks nothing like the adult, but a grasshopper's is incomplete because its nymph looks like a small adult.
A tadpole eats plants in water, but an adult frog eats insects on land, so its food changes with each stage.
Earthquakes happen most often along plate boundaries, which is why the Philippines experiences many of them.
The Philippines lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a long crack in the ground where two plates slide past each other sideways.
Mayon Volcano's perfect cone grew from lava and ash pushed up where the Eurasian Plate meets the Philippine Sea Plate.
Taal Volcano sits inside a caldera formed by an ancient eruption, marking the plate boundary zone in Luzon.
The Marikina Valley Fault is an active fault line running through Metro Manila that moves because of plate pressure.
Ocean trenches are the deepest places on Earth, and the Philippine Trench reaches about 10,000 meters down.
PHIVOLCS, the Philippine volcano and earthquake agency, watches the ground to track what the moving plates are doing.
Convergent boundaries push plates together, divergent boundaries pull them apart, and the Philippines has both convergent and transform boundaries.
The Philippine archipelago itself was built by millions of years of volcanic eruptions and plate collisions.
Seafloor spreading makes new ocean crust at mid-ocean ridges, while subduction destroys old crust at trenches.
In a tropical rainforest, dead leaves and wood rot quickly in the warm, wet conditions, so nutrients are recycled fast.
Many monkeys, birds, and insects live in the rainforest canopy, the top layer of leaves, and rarely come down to the ground.
An estuary is a place where a river meets the sea, mixing fresh water with salt water to make brackish water.
Many young fish and crabs grow up in estuaries because the shallow, calm water hides them from bigger predators.
Mangrove trees have roots that stick up out of the mud to get air because the soil is waterlogged and lacks oxygen.
Mangrove forests protect coastlines by slowing down waves and trapping soil, which reduces damage from storms and floods.
Mangrove trees survive in salty water by pushing extra salt out through their leaves or storing it in old bark.
Coral reefs are made by tiny animals called coral polyps that build hard skeletons from calcium carbonate in seawater.
Most reef corals have tiny algae living inside them that give the coral food and their bright colors.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor but are home to about one quarter of all marine species.
A swamp is different from a marsh because a swamp has trees, while a marsh is mostly grasses and reeds.
The Philippines is part of the Coral Triangle, the area with the highest coral reef biodiversity in the world.
When magma erupts on the deep ocean floor, it cools instantly into rounded pillow-shaped rocks that pile up to form the top layer of new oceanic crust.
The Philippines has about 300 volcanoes, and only about 24 are active, so most of the mountains you see are inactive.
A dormant volcano is quiet but could erupt again, while an extinct volcano has cooled down and is very unlikely to ever erupt.
The Philippines has many volcanoes because one piece of Earth's crust slides under another near the country, melting rock into magma.
Magma collects in a pocket underground called a magma chamber, and when pressure builds, it pushes up and erupts through the volcano.
Volcanic ash is made of tiny sharp fragments of rock and glass, so it is not soft like the ash from burned wood.
Volcanic soil is rich in minerals, so many farms in the Philippines grow good crops on the slopes of old, inactive volcanoes.
PHIVOLCS is the Philippine government agency that studies volcanoes and keeps the official list of which ones are active or inactive.
Moon phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it travels around Earth.
At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so the entire sunlit face of the Moon points toward us.
A half moon, called first quarter, occurs when the Moon is at a right angle to the line from Earth to the Sun.
Right after new moon, a thin crescent appears; it is just a small sliver of the Moon's sunlit side facing Earth.
A gibbous moon looks more than half lit but less than full, appearing between the half and full phases.
Waxing means the lit part of the Moon grows each night; waning means it shrinks, from full back to new.
Swamps provide feeding and nesting grounds for many birds, such as herons and egrets, that wade in the shallow water.
Mangrove roots are home to many animals like crabs, mudskippers, and monitor lizards that climb and dig among the tangled roots.
In any collision, the total momentum of all objects together stays the same before and after, even when they bounce or stick.
A car's crumple zone lengthens the time of a crash, and a longer stopping time means a smaller force on the people inside.
An airbag cushions a person by making the head slow down over a longer time, so the force of the stop is much smaller.
The Zambales ophiolite is a slab of ancient ocean floor now on land, evidence that seafloor was pushed up by plate collisions.
Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption, which sent ash high into the sky, happened because the Eurasian Plate is subducting beneath the Manila Trench.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a long transform fault that runs from Luzon to Mindanao, moving sideways as the plates grind past each other.
The Tiwi Geothermal Plant in Albay uses heat from plate boundaries to make electricity, showing that underground heat is close to the surface.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a system of many parallel faults, not just one crack, that run across the islands and cause earthquakes.
The volcanic rocks in the Philippines, like andesite and basalt, come from magma formed when subducted plates melt.
The Philippine Sea Plate's movement is causing the island of Luzon to rotate slowly clockwise over millions of years.
During an eruption, ash falls mostly on the side where the wind blows, so a town downwind of a volcano gets heavier ash than a town upwind at the same distance.
After a major eruption, PHIVOLCS redraws hazard maps because new craters and valleys change where lava and lahar can flow.
If heavy rain falls on fresh volcanic ash, it can form lahar, so towns near rivers face higher risk during typhoons after an eruption.
Carry a microscope with one hand on its arm and the other under its base to keep it safe.
Always center the specimen in the low power view before switching to a higher power lens.
To see animal cells, gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean toothpick and spread it on a slide.
For a reaction that needs electricity, scientists write the word 'electricity' above the arrow to show the energy source.
To write a formula equation for a metal and acid reaction, scientists write the metal symbol, plus acid formula, yields salt formula and H2.
To write a formula equation for a carbonate and acid reaction, scientists write the carbonate formula, plus acid formula, yields salt, H2O, and CO2.
Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean cotton swab and smear it on a slide to see animal cells.
Methylene blue dye stains the nucleus of cheek cells blue, making it easy to spot among the lighter cytoplasm.
Use the coarse focus knob only with the low power lens to bring the specimen into rough view without crashing the lens.
A good observation record includes a labeled drawing of the cell parts and the magnification number of the lens used.
Lower the coverslip at a 45-degree angle onto the water drop to push air bubbles out and keep the view clear.
Always center the specimen in the middle of the low power view before switching to high power so it stays in sight.
Use special lens paper to wipe the microscope lenses, because other cloths can scratch the glass and blur the image.
In a living cell, you may see tiny particles moving in the cytoplasm, which shows that the cell is active and not dead.
Household vinegar is a safe acid for the fizz test, bubbling on rocks that contain calcite.
A rock is a mixture of minerals, so the key asks about the whole rock's features, not one crystal.
Oceanic crust is the thin, heavy rock that forms the sea floor, made mostly of a dark rock called basalt.
Continental crust is the thick, lighter rock that makes up the land we live on, composed mostly of granite.
Earthquakes mostly happen where Earth's plates push, pull, or slide past each other, because the rocks suddenly break and shake.
When two pieces of continental crust collide, neither sinks, so they crumple and fold upward to form tall mountain belts like the Himalayas.
A curved chain of volcanoes, called a volcanic arc, builds up on the continental crust directly above where the oceanic plate slides down.
The Ring of Fire is a huge horse-shoe shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean where many volcanoes and earthquakes are found.
PHIVOLCS is the Philippine agency that maps active volcanoes and faults, helping people know where earthquakes and eruptions may happen.
Taal volcano sits inside a lake on Luzon, and its location is linked to the crack where two tectonic plates meet nearby.
The Andes mountains in South America formed where the dense oceanic Nazca plate dives beneath the lighter continental crust.
The Mariana Trench is the deepest part of the ocean, where heavy oceanic crust bends and sinks down into the mantle.
The Philippines sits where the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate push against each other, causing many earthquakes and volcanoes.
Where oceanic crust sinks, it drags the sea floor down to form a deep trench, like a giant underwater crack.
Liquid particles slide past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius, when liquid particles throughout the water gain enough energy to form bubbles of gas.
Condensation is when gas particles lose energy, slow down, and stick together to form a liquid, like drops on a cold glass.
Freezing happens when a liquid cools and its particles slow down enough to lock into fixed positions, forming a solid.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide that turns directly into gas without melting, a process called sublimation.
Frost on leaves forms when water vapor in the air turns directly into ice without becoming liquid first.
Gas particles have the most energy, liquid particles have less, and solid particles have the least energy of all.
